newsitem.title: UK: Small pro-British party quits N. Ireland talks.
newsitem.headline: Small pro-British party quits N. Ireland talks.

text.p: The smallest of Northern Ireland's three pro-British unionist parties said on Monday that it was pulling out of peace talks in protest at Britain's handling of the issue of IRA weapons.
The UK Unionist Party, led by lawyer Robert McCartney, made the announcement at Stormont buildings in Belfast, where the fragile year-old peace talks are under way.
He accused Britain of "terror appeasement" by allowing Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA (Irish Republican Army), to take part in the Belfast talks without the IRA surrendering any weapons.
Another small unionist group committed to British rule of Northern Ireland, the Democratic Unionist Party, has hinted that it will also walk out of the talks.

McCartney announced his decision as the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party led by David Trimble was about to hold talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair to protest at Britain's handling of the issue of "arms decommissioning".

McCartney said: "The representatives of political terror have been strengthened at the expense of democratic politicians and the confidence of the pro-Union people that the government will protect their constitutional rights has never ever been lower."
Unionism take its name from 300-year-old links between mainland Britain and Northern Ireland which were enshrined in the government of Ireland act of 1925 which declared the province British.
Each of the unionist parties has three seats at the Belfast talks.
If all three withdrew, the negotiations would not have the required consensus to reach a settlement to the 28-year dispute under ground rules worked out 13 months ago.
